name: Wildlife & Fisheries Management

objectives.text: Identify common local wildlife and fish species by their appearance, tracks, or sounds
Sort animals into game animals, fish caught for food, and protected species
Describe how food, water, cover, and space together make up a habitat that keeps wildlife populations healthy
Explain how predators and prey affect each other's numbers in a wildlife habitat
Describe the work of state wildlife agencies, biologists, and game wardens in protecting wildlife and fish
Explain how hunting seasons, bag limits, and fishing licenses help keep wildlife and fish populations at healthy levels
Explain carrying capacity and how limiting factors in a habitat cap the size of a wildlife population
Explain safe, legal, and ethical practices for hunting and fishing based on hunter and angler education principles
Describe how hunting and fishing license fees and excise taxes on sporting equipment fund wildlife and fisheries conservation
Explain how endangered species laws and recovery programs protect threatened wildlife and fish
Investigate a method used to estimate a wildlife or fish population, such as mark and recapture, transect counts, or electrofishing surveys
Describe how fish hatcheries and stocking programs are used to restore or supplement fish populations
Explain how invasive species such as feral hogs, invasive carp, and zebra mussels harm native wildlife and fisheries and how they are controlled
Apply identification techniques such as dichotomous keys, field guides, tracks, and sign to determine the species of wildlife and fish
Identify the characteristics of healthy wildlife habitat on a local site using a habitat evaluation scorecard
Compare sustainable harvest tools such as quotas, antlerless permits, slot limits, catch and release, and gear restrictions by their effect on population structure
Plan a supervised agricultural experience in wildlife or fisheries management, such as habitat improvement, pond management, or game bird production, with measurable goals and records
Analyze population and harvest data to judge whether a game or fish species is being managed sustainably
Assess wildlife harvest techniques for sustainability, practicality, ethics, and public acceptance

Analyze local wildlife populations and challenges to agricultural production, such as crop damage, livestock predation, and disease shared between wildlife and livestock, along with the control measures in use
Classify the causes of wildlife and aquatic species diseases as parasitic, bacterial, viral, fungal, or environmental
Analyze a wildlife or aquatic species disease such as chronic wasting disease or whirling disease based on its symptoms
Assess wildlife habitat management methods such as prescribed burning, food plots, edge creation, water development, and fish habitat structures
Evaluate the wildlife, fish, and aquatic insect species present at a site to assess the status of the ecosystem
Evaluate wildlife movement, invasive species spread, and habitat edge versus interior using GIS, GPS, and mapping tools
Develop recommendations for the sustainable harvest of an aquatic species in a farm pond, lake, or commercial fishery
Design a wildlife management plan that sets harvest methods, harvest limits, and habitat goals for a species based on its population ecology, density, and dispersion
Create a management plan to reduce the infection and spread of a wildlife or aquatic species disease
Evaluate the biodiversity of a wildlife habitat and devise strategies to increase it so the ecosystem supports healthier wildlife and fish populations

changes: Kept all six existing objectives as real competencies, rewording several (grade 2 sort, grade 4 habitat, grade 8 population estimation with field examples, grade 12 plan expanded to population ecology). Added early grade species identification, predator-prey, agency roles, carrying capacity, hunter ethics, conservation funding, endangered species, hatcheries and stocking, and invasive species. Added grade 9 to 12 objectives aligned to AFNR standards on species identification, habitat assessment and management, harvest regulation tools and technique assessment, aquatic harvest recommendations, wildlife-agriculture conflicts, disease classification, diagnosis, and management, indicator species, GIS mapping, and biodiversity, plus a wildlife or fisheries SAE planning objective. Soil, water, forestry, and rangeland content was left to sibling sub-topics.
